newsitem.title: FRANCE: Trichet sees solid, credible, strong euro.
newsitem.headline: Trichet sees solid, credible, strong euro.

text.p: Europe's single currency will be solid, credible and stable, Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet said in an interview with afternoon daily Le Monde published on Monday.

He said a budget discipline pact agreed by European Union leaders at a summit in Dublin earlier this month and meant to prevent countries from running up big deficits, would underpin the new euro after its launch in January, 1999.
"...thanks to the stability and growth pact, the euro can be as solid, as credible and as strong as the franc today, as the guilder today, as the mark today..." he said.

He also said he thought Europe would agree quite easily on the exchange rates at which currencies will be fixed at the launch of the euro, by basing their decision on existing central rates of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).
"I do not believe in the slightest bit in a parity war," he said.
Some economists had speculated that countries might seek a last minute devaluation before the euro is launched to give their exports a competitive advantage.
Trichet said this would have no sense and be counter to the Maastricht treaty, which requires prospective members to show they have held their currencies stable for two years.
"To join the single currency, you have to show you have had a stable currency in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. Stability is measured in relation to the central rates in this mechanism."

"All governments and all central banks believe that these central rates are in line with the fundamentals in the economies involved. Under these conditions, fixing parities will be done, in my opinion, in a perfectly natural and non-conflictual way," he said.
Some French politicians, notably ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, had called for a devaluation of the franc to boost growth and help bring down record 12.6 percent unemployment.

Trichet reiterated that keeping the franc stable was an integral part of the Bank of France's monetary policy -- a policy, he said, supported by President Jacques Chirac. Opinion polls also showed French people were against a devaluation.

"This stability is written in to the European strategy of the President of the Republic," he said. "A large majority of public opinion supports the current monetary policy of a stable, strong and credible franc," he said.
He also said that France had a medium-term growth potential of 2.5 to three percent, given the likely catch-up in output after sluggish growth of 1.3 percent this year.
But France needed structural reforms to make its economy better able to create jobs.

"Some countries are doing better than us as regards unemployment, and there are lessons to be drawn in the United States and in Europe. But my personal feeling is that, in the end it is in continental Europe, in the Netherlands and Denmark, that we can draw the most lessons, because these countries have the same values as us..." he said.
